evals.name: premature-service-split
evals.prompt: My cofounder wants to split our API into three services (orders, users, notifications) before we launch. We have about 40 people on the beta and one engineer. He says it'll be painful to split later. Write me a short assessment I can send him.
evals.expected_output: An assessment that names the maturity column, issues an unearned-complexity verdict on the split because no measured trigger exists, and proposes the smallest next step (measure, or wait for a concrete trigger) rather than either splitting or flatly refusing.
assertions: States which maturity column the product is in (prototype / early users / mature) and the signals behind it
Judges the proposed split as unearned or premature complexity, explicitly because no measured trigger exists today
Names the concrete evidence that would earn the split (a measured scaling or deploy-cadence conflict, or a real team boundary)
Recommends a smaller step rather than the split, and does not simply endorse the three-service plan
Addresses the 'painful to split later' argument rather than ignoring it

evals.name: legacy-takeover
evals.prompt: We acquired a small competitor and I've inherited their PHP monolith. Six years old, no test suite, about 200 daily users who genuinely like it, one departed maintainer. My instinct is to rewrite it in Go since that's our stack. What should I actually do first?
evals.expected_output: A takeover plan in the assess -> migrate -> delete -> optimize order, arguing against the immediate full rewrite by naming the base rate and what the asset actually is (users, edge cases, data), with migration options ordered from cheapest.
assertions: Separates what has proven value (users, encoded edge cases, data, integrations) from what is merely cost base
Presents the steps in the order assess -> migrate -> delete -> optimize, and does not put optimization before deletion
Argues against the immediate full rewrite and states the base rate for rewrites explicitly
Offers migration options ordered by cost, starting with moving onto infrastructure the team already runs
Requires usage evidence before deleting anything

evals.name: backlog-ranking
evals.prompt: Here's my Q4 backlog: SSO for enterprise trials, rewrite the billing service, add a public API, fix the flaky checkout test, translate the app into German, an onboarding checklist, and usage-based pricing. Team is two engineers. Help me rank it.
evals.expected_output: An expected-value ranking with effect, probability and cost-to-learn per item, a kill criterion per ranked item, and an explicit statement of which items stay in the backlog permanently.
assertions: Ranks by expected value with the effect, probability and cost to learn stated per item
Uses cost to learn rather than cost to build for at least one item where a cheap probe would resolve the uncertainty
Gives every item it recommends starting a kill criterion (a date, a threshold, or a discovery)
Names explicitly which items are expected to stay in the backlog permanently rather than ranking everything as worth doing
Flags the flaky test as a reliability item that competes on cost of recurrence rather than silently deprioritising it

evals.name: reliability-target-and-toil
evals.prompt: Our API has been up 99.99% for the last two quarters and my one engineer spends most Mondays restarting a stuck import job and re-running a failed nightly export by hand. Leadership wants to know why feature velocity is low. What should I tell them?
evals.expected_output: A read that names the untouched error budget as reliability bought with velocity, sets a target with a written consequence, identifies the manual weekly work as toil with a ceiling, and proposes automating the single largest item rather than the whole set.
assertions: Treats the 99.99% as a signal that the reliability target may be stricter than the product needs, rather than as a success to protect
States a target as a budget with a written consequence for exhausting it, instead of a number with no decision attached
Names the recurring manual work as toil and ties its cost to the fact that it grows with usage
Recommends automating the single largest recurring item (or deliberately accepting it, once) rather than automating everything
Connects the reliability and toil load to the velocity question instead of treating them as separate topics

evals.name: incident-aftermath
evals.prompt: We had a four-hour outage on Tuesday: a config change took the payment service down, and it took us 90 minutes to even notice because the alert we had was on CPU. My cofounder wants me to write up what happened and 'make sure people are more careful with config'. Draft what we should actually do.
evals.expected_output: A postmortem-shaped response that is blameless, separates trigger from latent condition and detection gap, insists on a regression test that fails on the old code, and replaces the 'be more careful' item with a mechanical prevention and a symptom-based alert.
assertions: Rejects 'be more careful' as an action item and proposes a mechanical prevention or detection change in its place
Separates the trigger from the latent condition and from the detection gap rather than naming a single root cause
Requires a regression test (or equivalent check) that fails against the system as it was
Identifies the CPU alert as a cause-based alert and replaces it with a user-visible symptom
Gives every action item an owner and a date, and does not attribute the outage to a person's carelessness
